questions.prompt: Select every true statement about what a Salesforce 'application' actually is, per this course.
options: An app is a curated container of tabs, branding, and visibility — not separate software or a separate codebase.
Every app, standard or custom, shows up in the same App Launcher grid with no visual distinction.
App Manager in Setup is the admin's master list of every app in the org.
A custom app requires its own separate database, distinct from the org's shared data model.
Only Salesforce-shipped apps can appear in the App Launcher grid.
questions.explain: An app is configuration, not code — a curated container built on the one platform the org already runs. Standard and custom apps both appear in the same App Launcher grid with no distinction, and App Manager is the admin's master list of every app. There's no separate database per app, and custom apps appear in the App Launcher exactly like standard ones.

questions.prompt: Put these four stages of the New Lightning App wizard, per this course, in the order they appear.
items: Navigation Items — which tabs ship, and in what order
User Profiles — which profiles can open the app
questions.explain: The New Lightning App wizard runs through Details, Branding, Navigation Items (moving tabs from Available Items into Selected Items), and finally User Profiles — in exactly that order, with no code at any stage.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks for 'a place to track customer complaints.' Per this course's declarative-first design order, what should you check before deciding anything else?
options: Whether a standard object or field already covers the requirement, before building anything custom.
Whether Apex can be written fast enough to meet the deadline.
Whether a Lightning web component already exists for complaints.
Whether the requirement needs a new Salesforce edition purchased.
questions.explain: The declarative-first design order starts with reusing a standard object before building a custom one, then a standard field, then configuring before customizing, and customizing before anyone writes Apex — the reuse check runs at every step, starting with the very first one.

questions.prompt: Per this course's rule for choosing between lookup and master-detail relationships, which pairing calls for master-detail?
options: An Opportunity Line Item and its Opportunity, since a line item can't exist without it.
A Contact and an Opportunity it was once related to, since a Contact can outlive that specific deal.
An Opportunity Line Item and its Opportunity, since master-detail is required whenever a roll-up summary isn't needed.
A Case and the Account it's filed against, since every Case must inherit the Account's exact page layout.
A Lead and the Campaign that originated it, since Leads can never exist without a Campaign record.
A Contact and its Account, since master-detail is always used whenever two standard objects relate to each other.
questions.explain: The rule is existence dependency: choose master-detail only when the child record genuinely cannot exist without its parent. An Opportunity Line Item has no meaning without its Opportunity, which is exactly the master-detail case this course names directly.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C also names the correct pairing — Opportunity Line Item to Opportunity — but gives the wrong reason. The deciding factor is whether the child can exist without the parent, not whether a roll-up summary happens to be needed. A roll-up summary is something master-detail makes possible as a consequence, not the reason to choose it in the first place.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a custom object with two master-detail (or lookup) relationships, one to each side of a many-to-many relationship, is called a ________.
questions.explain: A many-to-many relationship can't be modeled with a single field — it needs a junction object sitting between the two sides, with a relationship to each. In the warranty-claims model, Claim_Line_Item__c is that junction, linking Warranty_Claim__c to Product2.

questions.prompt: A requirement says 'track which employees attended which training sessions, and let a session have a pass/fail score per employee.' Per this course, is that one-to-many or many-to-many, and what extra object is needed?
options: Many-to-many — a junction object (like Attendance) is needed to hold the per-employee, per-session pass/fail score, since that data can't live on Employee or Session alone.
One-to-many — Session simply gets a lookup field pointing at one Employee.
Many-to-many — no extra object is needed, since Employee and Session can reference each other directly with a single shared field.
One-to-many — Employee gets a master-detail relationship directly to Training_Session__c with no other object involved.
questions.explain: Many employees attend many sessions, and each other, each attendance-score needs. That score is relationship-specific data that can't live on Employee or Session alone — exactly the shape that requires a junction object, the same pattern as CampaignMember linking Contacts to Campaigns.

questions.prompt: Match each field type to what it enforces, per this course.
right: Always correct — no one has to remember to update it manually
Nothing — every typo becomes a stored, reportable value
Only the values you defined can ever be entered
Can never drift out of sync with the fields it's calculated from
questions.explain: Free text enforces nothing. A Picklist restricts entry to defined values. A Formula field can never drift out of sync since it's recalculated live. A Roll-up summary is always correct because no one has to remember to update it manually — each step trades flexibility for data quality.

questions.prompt: A user says, 'I added a field to the Account page layout, but it's not showing up when I hover an Account from a Contact.' What's actually missing, and which tool fixes it?
options: The field isn't in the compact layout, which is what powers hover cards — adding it to the page layout alone doesn't affect the compact layout.
The field needs field-level security granted on the Contact object instead of Account.
Hover cards only ever show the Account Name field and can never be customized.
The page layout assignment needs to be reset for the user's profile.
questions.explain: Hover cards are powered by the compact layout's chosen fields, not the page layout. Adding a field to the page layout only affects the full record page — the compact layout has to be edited separately for it to show up in a hover card, the highlights panel, or the mobile record view.

questions.prompt: Per this course, what is the single most common mix-up Platform App Builder exam-takers make regarding page layouts and compact layouts?
options: Assuming the highlights panel pulls its fields from the page layout, when it's actually powered by the compact layout.
Assuming the highlights panel pulls its fields from the compact layout, when it's actually powered by the page layout.
Assuming a compact layout can include related lists, when related lists are actually page layout only.
Assuming a page layout can show more than 10 fields, when the limit is actually enforced on page layouts too.
Assuming compact layouts control which actions appear in the action overflow menu.
Assuming page layouts are configured in Lightning App Builder instead of Object Manager.
questions.explain: The course names this directly: assuming the highlights panel pulls from the page layout — when it's actually the compact layout that powers the highlights panel, mobile record view, and hover cards — is the single most common mistake exam-takers make.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B states the exact same confusion with the two tools swapped. It's the compact layout, not the page layout, that powers the highlights panel, mobile view, and hover cards — the page layout controls the full record page's fields, sections, related lists, and buttons. Getting the direction backwards is exactly the mix-up this lesson warns against.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Lightning App Builder's three page types, per this course.
options: An App Page serves as a custom home page for one specific app.
A Record Page overrides the standard layout for one object.
A Home Page replaces the org-wide Lightning home screen.
A Record Page requires Apex to display any related list.
All three page types require a separate mobile-specific build.
questions.explain: App Page, Record Page, and Home Page are the three page types, matching exactly those three descriptions. Related lists don't require Apex to display on a Record Page, and Lightning pages render on both desktop and mobile from a single build — no separate mobile-specific construction needed.

questions.prompt: A sales manager wants junior reps to see a 'Discount Approved By' field only when Discount Percent exceeds 20%, without building a second page layout. How does Dynamic Forms solve this?
options: Migrate the field to a component on the Lightning page and set a component visibility rule filtering on Discount Percent > 20%.
Create a validation rule that hides the field whenever Discount Percent is 20% or below.
Add a second compact layout that only junior reps are assigned to.
Use a Formula field to blank out the Discount Approved By value until the threshold is met.
questions.explain: Once a field is a Dynamic Forms component, it can carry its own visibility rule — a filter evaluated against the record that decides whether the field renders at all. That's a per-field, declarative condition set directly on the component, with no second page layout, Apex, or validation-rule workaround needed.

questions.prompt: A support rep wants a one-click 'Log a Call' button available from every screen in the org, not just from a Case record. Is that a global action or an object-specific action?
options: A global action, since it needs no record context and must be reachable from anywhere.
An object-specific action, since Log a Call is always scoped to the Case object specifically.
Neither — quick actions can only be added to page layouts, not the global header.
An object-specific action, since every quick action requires an open record to run.
questions.explain: A global action is reachable from anywhere in the org, with no record context required, through the plus icon in the header. An object-specific action is scoped to one object type and only appears on that object's records — the opposite of what this rep is asking for.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a developer-defined setting on a custom Lightning component that a Platform App Builder can configure without writing code — like which list it shows — is called an ________ property.
questions.explain: An exposed property is a setting the developer deliberately made configurable. The App Builder sets these in the Page properties panel — deciding WHERE a component goes and configuring its exposed properties, without needing to write or understand the component's own code.

questions.prompt: A manager wants Dashboards to be one tap away on mobile, but doesn't care where it sits in the desktop nav bar. Where do you make that change, and why won't editing the desktop order alone do it?
options: In the app's Activation dialog, on the dedicated Mobile Navigation tab — mobile menu order is set completely independently of the desktop nav bar, so the first four items on mobile come from that separate setting.
In the desktop Navigation Items list, since mobile always mirrors whatever order is set there.
In each user's personal Settings, since mobile tab order is a per-user preference with no admin control.
In the Compact Layout editor, since the bottom tab bar is powered by the compact layout's field order.
questions.explain: The Activation dialog's Mobile Navigation tab sets the mobile menu order independently of the desktop nav bar. Since the first four items in that mobile list also populate the bottom tab bar, this explicit, admin-controlled setting — not the desktop order — is what determines what's one tap away.

questions.prompt: A record is created, and a validation rule and a Flow both reference the same field. The Flow is supposed to set that field to a value that would otherwise satisfy the validation rule, but the rule evaluates first in the save order. Will the save succeed?
options: No — the validation rule only ever evaluates the record as it stands at save time, before the Flow runs, so it can block the save even though the Flow would have set a satisfying value afterward.
Yes — Salesforce always re-runs validation rules after every Flow finishes, so the Flow's update is checked too.
Yes — validation rules are skipped entirely whenever any Flow references the same field.
No — Flows always run before validation rules in Salesforce's order of execution.
questions.explain: Validation rules run early in the save order and only ever see the record as it stands at that moment. A later Flow step can't retroactively satisfy a rule that already blocked the save — a validation rule can never see a value a later Flow is about to set.

questions.prompt: You need a validation rule that fires when a Task's Status is 'Completed' but its Due Date is still blank. Which Error Condition Formula correctly implements that?
options: AND( ISPICKVAL(Status, "Completed"), ISBLANK(DueDate) )
OR( ISPICKVAL(Status, "Completed"), ISBLANK(DueDate) )
AND( ISCHANGED(Status), ISBLANK(DueDate) )
NOT( AND( ISPICKVAL(Status, "Completed"), ISBLANK(DueDate) ) )
questions.explain: A validation rule fires on TRUE, so the formula should describe the bad condition directly: Status is Completed AND DueDate is blank, combined with AND(). OR() would fire too broadly (either condition alone), ISCHANGED() checks whether Status changed rather than its current value, and wrapping the whole thing in NOT() would invert the rule to fire in exactly the wrong cases.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about formula fields, per this course.
options: A formula field's value isn't stored in the database — it's computed whenever the record is viewed, reported on, or queried.
A formula field can reference fields on a related object through dot notation, like Account.Industry.
A formula field can be the target of a Data Loader import.
A formula field can have its own field history tracking, the same as a stored field.
BLANKVALUE() substitutes a default value when a field is empty.
questions.explain: A formula field isn't stored and recalculates on read, and it can reach across relationships with dot notation like Account.Industry. BLANKVALUE() substitutes a default for an empty field. It can't be targeted by a Data Loader import (there's no stored value to write to) and can't have field history tracking, since it's never 'changed,' only recalculated.

questions.prompt: A Project__c object needs to know how many Task__c records are overdue. Task__c is detail in a master-detail relationship to Project__c. What roll-up summary field setup, per this course, correctly answers this?
options: A COUNT roll-up on Project__c, from the Task__c relationship, with filter criteria limiting it to overdue tasks.
A SUM roll-up on Task__c, from the Project__c relationship, totaling the Project's own due dates.
A formula field on Project__c that recalculates a stored count every time any Task__c is viewed.
A COUNT roll-up on Task__c, since roll-up summary fields are always built on the detail object.
questions.explain: A roll-up summary field is built on the master object, aggregating from its detail children — here, a COUNT on Project__c from its Task__c children, filtered to only count overdue tasks. Roll-ups live on the master, not the detail, and a formula field has no stored value to maintain an aggregate count in the first place.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Salesforce ships one standard junction object out of the box, linking Opportunities and Contacts many-to-many, called ________.
questions.explain: OpportunityContactRole is Salesforce's standard junction object linking Opportunities and Contacts many-to-many — the same pattern a custom junction object like Enrollment__c implements for Students and Courses.

questions.prompt: A time-off request should require manager approval only if requested days exceed the employee's remaining balance, which depends on a running total from other records. Why can't a plain approval process's entry criteria alone handle this, and what role does Flow play?
options: Entry criteria is a simple filter and can't evaluate a running total across other records — a Flow calculates that comparison first, then decides whether to call Submit for Approval.
Approval processes can't be used for time-off requests at all, since they only apply to Opportunities and Cases.
Entry criteria can reference a running total natively, so Flow isn't actually needed here.
Flow replaces the approval process entirely, since Flow can also lock records and show Approval History.
questions.explain: Entry criteria is a static, report-like filter — it can't evaluate a rolling total from other records. A Flow can run that calculation and decide whether approval is even needed, then call Submit for Approval to hand the record to the approval process for the actual routing, locking, and audit trail.

questions.prompt: Put these questions from this course's automation-tool decision path in the order you'd ask them.
items: Does this only need to stop a bad save? -> Validation rule
Does this only need to display a calculated value, never store it? -> Formula field
Does this need a stored aggregate from direct child records? -> Roll-up summary field
Does this need one or more named humans to explicitly sign off? -> Approval process
Does this need multiple steps, branching, loops, or a screen? -> Flow
Does it still not fit after all five? -> Apex
questions.explain: The decision path runs in this order: block, then calculate, then aggregate, then route for approval, then branch/loop/act with Flow, and only then reach for Apex when none of the five declarative tools fit.

questions.prompt: Match each requirement to the tool this course's decision framework resolves it to.
left: Block saving a Case with no Description
Total value of all open Opportunities on an Account
Director sign-off before a Contract over $100K activates
questions.explain: Blocking a save with no side effect is a validation rule. A calculated, never-stored value is a formula field. A stored aggregate from direct children is a roll-up summary field. A named human sign-off with an audit trail is an approval process — each requirement maps to exactly one tool based on whether it blocks, calculates, aggregates, or routes.

questions.prompt: A manager wants one dashboard showing open Request counts broken down by both Owner and Priority, where each rep who views it only sees their own records. Which report format and dashboard setting fit?
options: A matrix report (grouped by Owner and Priority at once), with the dashboard set to run dynamically as the logged-in user.
A tabular report with no grouping, run as a single specified user for consistency.
A summary report grouped only by Priority, run as a specified user who is a System Administrator.
A joined report combining Owner and Priority as two separate unrelated blocks, run as the dashboard's creator.
questions.explain: A matrix report groups by rows and columns at once — exactly 'Owner by Priority.' Running the dashboard dynamically as the logged-in user means each rep's own sharing and field-level security apply, so they see only their own records instead of everyone seeing the dashboard creator's access.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about report formats, per this course.
options: A tabular report is a flat list, fastest to build, with no subtotals.
A summary report groups rows with subtotals at each grouping level.
A matrix report groups by rows and columns at once, producing a cross-tab.
A joined report can only combine blocks from the exact same object, never different objects.
A dashboard component queries its own data directly, independent of any report.
questions.explain: Tabular, summary, and matrix formats match exactly those three descriptions. A joined report can combine blocks from related or even unrelated objects, not just the same object, and a dashboard component doesn't query data itself — it visualizes a source report's results.

questions.prompt: A custom object's OWD is Private. A support rep is not the record owner, not above the owner in the role hierarchy, and has full object and field access on their permission set. Can they see a specific record, and what would need to change for them to see it?
options: No — object and field access alone don't grant record-level access under Private OWD; a sharing rule, role hierarchy position, or manual share would need to extend access to that specific record.
Yes — full object and field access automatically overrides Private OWD for any user.
No — Private OWD can never be overridden by any mechanism, including sharing rules, once set.
Yes — Private OWD only restricts field-level access, never record-level access.
questions.explain: Security is layered, not additive in the forgiving sense: a user needs object access AND field access AND record access. Full object and field access doesn't substitute for record-level access under Private OWD — a sharing rule, role hierarchy position, or manual share is needed to extend visibility to that specific record.

questions.prompt: A validation rule references a new custom field that doesn't exist yet in production. You add only the validation rule to an outbound change set and upload it. What happens, and why does the dependency step matter?
options: The deployment fails validation, because the change set doesn't include the custom field the validation rule depends on — dependencies have to be added to the same change set.
The deployment succeeds, and Salesforce automatically creates the missing field in production with default settings.
The deployment succeeds, but the validation rule is silently deactivated until the field is added later.
The deployment succeeds, since change sets validate only syntax, not whether referenced fields exist.
questions.explain: Adding components to an outbound change set also requires adding their dependencies — a Flow or validation rule that references a custom field needs that field added too, or the deployment fails validation. Salesforce checks these dependencies rather than silently working around a missing one.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a sandbox type that's a complete copy of both metadata and data, used for staging, performance testing, and final UAT before production, is called a ________ sandbox.
questions.explain: A Full sandbox is a complete copy of metadata and data, used for staging, performance testing, and final UAT — the richest, most production-like environment in the typical Developer -> Developer Pro -> Partial Copy/Full -> Production path.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about user experience and adoption, per this course.
options: Dynamic Actions can show a quick action like 'Submit for Approval' only when the record is actually eligible.
Salesforce's Optimizer app can surface unused fields and inactive validation rules.
Phasing rollout by permission set lets a pilot group test a new app before it's assigned to everyone at once.
Shipping a new app and confirming it's live is the same claim as confirming people are actually using it.
In-App Guidance Prompts require a developer to write custom Apex before they can be shown.
questions.explain: Dynamic Actions reduce friction by showing actions only when eligible, Optimizer surfaces unused fields and inactive rules, and phasing rollout by permission set lets a pilot group test first. 'We shipped it' is explicitly not the same claim as 'people use it,' and In-App Guidance Prompts are a declarative, no-code tool.

questions.prompt: In the Harborline Logistics case study, why is Maintenance_Request__c modeled as a separate custom object in a master-detail relationship to Vehicle__c, instead of as extra fields directly on Vehicle__c?
options: Because a single vehicle has many maintenance events over its life, and fields can't repeat — plus master-detail enables the roll-up totals the business wants on the vehicle later.
Because Salesforce doesn't allow custom fields to be added to a standard object like Vehicle__c.
Because a lookup relationship would have been cheaper, but master-detail was chosen arbitrarily.
Because Technician__c also needed a master-detail relationship to Vehicle__c, forcing Maintenance_Request__c to be separate.
questions.explain: A vehicle has many maintenance events over its lifetime — fields on a single record can't repeat — so a separate child object is required. Master-detail was chosen specifically because a maintenance request has no meaning without its vehicle, and because it enables the roll-up totals Harborline wants on the vehicle.

questions.prompt: In the Help Desk Ticket app, which Chapter 4 decision specifically ensures a technician can't see tickets assigned to a different technician's queue?
options: Private OWD on Help_Desk_Ticket__c combined with a sharing rule that grants the IT Queue, not individual technicians broadly, read/write access to all tickets.
The Dynamic Form that hides Asset__c until Priority__c is set.
The formula field calculating Hours_Open__c from CreatedDate.
The screen Flow that powers the Escalate quick action.
questions.explain: Private OWD means no visibility by default, and the sharing rule deliberately grants access to the IT Queue rather than broadly to every technician — that security combination, not any Chapter 2 or Chapter 3 decision, is what actually scopes which tickets a given technician can see.
